claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 at.% boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve their glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% boron will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state in these alloys.
Homogeneous boron distribution under rapid solidification is a condition under which the intervention should improve glass formation.
If the cooling rate is too low, the beneficial effect of boron may not occur.
Excess boron may eliminate the beneficial effect.
Boron interacting with phosphorus and the other principal elements will enhance local atomic packing.
Boron interacting with phosphorus and the other principal elements will enhance short-range chemical order.
The boron addition will increase atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Increased atomic-size disparity and chemical-bonding complexity will frustrate crystallization kinetics.
The boron-induced structural and chemical changes will raise the energy barrier for crystalline-phase nucleation.
The boron-induced structural and chemical changes will raise the energy barrier for crystalline-phase growth during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
Relative to a boron-free baseline, the boron-modified alloy should have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation.
Relative to a boron-free baseline, the boron-modified alloy should have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature.
The beneficial effect is restricted to a narrow boron concentration window of approximately 1–2 at.%.
The intervention may have no discernible effect in alloys lacking sufficient atomic-size mismatch.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in critical cooling rate and/or an increase in crystallization-onset temperature relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
